label: Status and Recognition
framing: The hunger to be recognized is not a modern invention, only a newly measured one, now counted in followers and likes. Scripture does not crush the desire to matter but reorders it, warning against doing good to be seen by others, and pointing the heart toward an audience of One who already sees in secret.
cultural: We have turned attention into a currency and made ourselves its anxious accountants, checking the numbers that tell us how much we are worth today. The platform offers a thin counterfeit of the recognition the soul actually craves, to be truly known and still loved, and we keep refreshing it because the counterfeit never satisfies.
historical: Jesus aimed his sharpest warnings at the religious leaders who loved the place of honor and the greeting in the marketplaces, doing their righteousness to be seen. Augustine confessed in the fourth century how even his preaching could be poisoned by the love of praise, and Jonathan Edwards in the eighteenth century probed how the desire for the esteem of others hides inside our holiest acts.
application: Practice doing good that no one will ever see, and let the secrecy starve the part of you that performs. Notice when your motive bends toward the applause and bring it back to God, the only audience that finally matters. Build your worth on being known and loved by him rather than tallied by strangers. And serve the people who can do nothing for your reputation, since that is where the disordered hunger goes to die.

verses.text: All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels. They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, the greetings in the marketplaces, and the title of ‘Rabbi’ by which they are addressed.
verses.where: Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees do their deeds to be seen, and love the best seats at banquets and synagogues, the greetings in the marketplace and the title Rabbi. The site's note says the list moves from private feasts to public worship to the street, every place a person can be seen, and that the love of rank is a temptation for every religious leader, not a peculiarity of the first century. The plain note says the warning lands first on those who teach and lead in his church today.

verses.text: But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place, so that your host will come and tell you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”
verses.where: Watching guests choose the places of honor, Jesus tells them to take the last place and let the host move them up, for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. The site's plain note says this is not a clever way to get honor in the end; honor is God's to give, and the humble person has stopped keeping score. It adds that humility is not thinking yourself worthless: the host calls the one in the last seat Friend.

verses.text: But it shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
verses.where: When James and John ask for the seats beside his throne, Jesus says that among his followers whoever wants to be great must be a servant, for the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. The site's note says Jesus defines leadership among his people against the pattern of political power. The plain note asks where you could serve this week in a way no one will notice or thank you for.

verses.text: “Come,” they said, “let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth.”
verses.where: The builders of Babel set out to build a tower to the heavens so that they may make a name for themselves and not be scattered. The site's note says their sin was not building or cooperating but seeking a name and a security of their own making, and that in the next chapter God promises to make Abram's name great. The plain note asks where you are trying to build a name, and what you fear will happen if you do not.

verses.text: I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction. So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church.
verses.where: The elder writes of Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first, slanders the elder and puts out of the church those who welcome travelling believers. The site's plain note says the letter answers by naming the wrong plainly and not answering slander with slander, and that it does not ask anyone to stay under a leader who controls, shames or harms them. It asks whether you have ever kept someone out to keep control.

verses.text: Haman entered, and the king asked him, “What should be done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor?” Now Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?”
verses.where: Asked by the king how to honor a man the king delights in, Haman thinks to himself that the king could mean no one but him. The site's note on the chapter says that, assuming he is the man, he describes a royal parade and is ordered to give that honor to Mordecai. The hunger to be recognized hears every compliment as its own.

verses.text: But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking! For I will bring disaster on every living creature, declares the LORD, but wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war.”
verses.where: God answers the complaint of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe: do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking. The site's note on the chapter says God himself was tearing down what he had built, and that what he promised Baruch was not success but survival. Faithful work in a hard time may never be the kind that is noticed.

verses.text: But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’ I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”
verses.where: The tax collector stands at a distance, beats his breast and asks only for mercy, and Jesus says he, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. The site's note says he compares himself to no one and brings no achievements. The plain note warns that the quickest way to become the Pharisee in the story is to thank God you are not like him, and says the parable speaks first to the church.

verses.text: So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you.
verses.where: Having washed his disciples' feet, Jesus tells them that if their Lord and Teacher has done this, they should wash one another's feet. The site's note says he does not give up his titles but shows what they mean: authority among his followers is measured by readiness to serve. The plain note asks what lowly, unseen, unthanked task you could do for someone this week without being asked.

verses.text: Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness. And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death— even death on a cross.
verses.where: Paul asks the church to have the mind of Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant and humbled himself to death on a cross. The site's plain note says what he set aside was clinging to the honor and rights that were his, and asks what rights or honors you hold on to tightly. Paul tells the story so that the church will treat one another the way Christ treated us.

links.label: Practical guides for life in the world

misread.taken: Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds is used to justify making sure one's giving, service or devotion is noticed, as though being seen were the point.
misread.says: The site's plain note sets the verse beside Jesus' warning in the next chapter not to perform righteous acts before others to be seen by them, and says the difference is the goal. Here the deeds are seen so that people glorify the Father in heaven; in chapter 6 they are done so that people will praise the one doing them. The question in both places, the note says, is who gets the glory.
misread.text: In the same way, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

whole: Almost everyone wants to matter to someone, and to have what they do noticed. The hunger shows itself in small ways: checking how many people liked a post, rehearsing a compliment, feeling a sting when a colleague is thanked in the meeting and you are not, wanting the title or the office or the seat near the front. In some it becomes a driving force, so that every room is an audience and every conversation a chance to be seen well. In others it hides behind modesty, the quiet resentment of the person who does the work no one praises. The desire is not wrong in itself. What goes wrong is where we look to have it met.

Scripture traces the trouble back to Babel, where the builders wanted to make a name for themselves, and the site's note says their sin was seeking a name and a security of their own making. Jesus watched guests scramble for the best seats, and he warned that the love of the best places, the greetings and the titles is a temptation for every religious leader. Haman heard the king's question and assumed it could only be about him. Even the twelve argued over who was greatest on the way to the cross. The common thread is that recognition from people has taken the place of the one verdict that lasts, so that a person's sense of worth rises and falls with the room.

So the Bible's wisdom reorders the desire rather than crushing it. Jesus tells his followers to take the lower place and let honor be God's to give, and the plain note says the humble person is not playing a longer game but has stopped keeping score. He washed feet and told his disciples to do the same, and the note asks for one unseen, unthanked task this week. Good deeds may be seen, but so that the Father is glorified, not the one who did them. Those who lead hear the warning first, as Diotrephes shows. And those who have been overlooked can hear God's word to Baruch, who was promised not success but his life, and was told to stop seeking great things for himself.

The hope Scripture gives is that the recognition the soul wants most is already offered. The host calls the guest in the last seat Friend. The tax collector, who brought nothing and compared himself to no one, went home justified. Christ emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and God gave him the name above every name, so the way down is not the way to nothing. A person who is known by God and received by him does not need to win the room, and is free at last to make much of someone else.
deep.sit: What good thing could you do this week that no one will ever know about, and what would it feel like to leave it that way?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says verse 1 asks whose glory you are after, and that not to us is a hard prayer for anyone and a good one to say slowly, and often.
prayer.text: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory, because of Your loving devotion, because of Your faithfulness.
